title: First-seen is not novelty; default novelty views must exclude baseline records by construction
requirement: A record's first appearance in a Clank's own database (its discovery/observation time) MUST NOT, by itself, be treated as evidence that the thing it represents is new in the real world. Any default or active view that a Clank uses to surface novelty — a new-item feed, a default alerting query, an editorial 'what's new' queue — MUST exclude baseline/continuity-tagged records (see STD-DATA-COM-001) by construction, i.e. via a read-side predicate evaluated at query time, not by relying on the record never having been written, on a caller remembering to filter, or on an upstream process having already removed them. Where a Clank models editorial freshness (is this item current enough to present as news) as a concept distinct from discovery-novelty, editorial freshness MUST remain a separate, further judgement — never implied by, or conflated with, either local discovery time or novelty status.
trigger: Applies to any Clank whose default/active views consume a novelty judgement (alerting, new-item feeds, editorial intake queues) derived from local history. A catalogue or full-history view that legitimately displays baseline records alongside current ones is not itself in scope — the exclusion binds novelty-consuming views specifically, not every view of the data. A Clank with no baseline/continuity concept at all (STD-DATA-COM-001's trigger unmet) has nothing to exclude and is out of scope by construction, not in violation. The editorial-freshness clause applies only where a Clank has modeled editorial freshness as a concept at all (typically news/lead-oriented Clanks) — a pure catalogue/SKU Clank is not required to build editorial freshness to conform to this standard.
rationale: This is the best-evidenced candidate in the entire Pass 0 corpus. The semantic distinction alone (first-seen != novelty) is necessary but proven insufficient: watch-clank and oem-radar independently suffered the identical failure — a baseline flag correctly written at discovery time, never consulted by the display/aggregation query that fed alerts — with zero cross-citation between the two repos. A representation-only standard would have been satisfied by both repos while the underlying bug persisted in both, because the flag existed; nothing required the read path to use it. The standardizable core is therefore the read-side contract, not just the write-side tagging, mirroring the same structural shape already ratified fleet-wide for QC queues (STD-UI-COM-003: a decided item must be excluded from the active queue via a read-side filter, not by deleting the record). Editorial freshness is folded in as a corollary because chinese-tech-wire's own architecture explicitly separates it from novelty scoring as a distinct question, and korean-tech-wire independently names the same gap in its own docs as unbuilt future work — but no SKU/catalogue Clank in the surveyed fleet has or needs an editorial-freshness concept, so it is not made a universal requirement.
forbidden: A default novelty/new-item/alerting view expressed as, in effect, 'ORDER BY first_seen DESC' with no baseline/continuity exclusion — presenting recency-of-observation as if it were novelty
A bootstrap or re-baseline flood becoming eligible for the 'new/novel' category merely because ingestion happened today
Depending on a caller, a cron job, or an operator to remember to filter baseline records out of a novelty view, where the query itself would otherwise return them

Excluding baseline records via logic external to the novelty-asserting path's own definition or its explicitly-inherited eligibility rule (e.g. a post-hoc application-layer filter applied after the path's results are produced) — even where this happens to work today, it leaves the path itself non-conforming and reintroduces the exact failure mode this standard exists to prevent
Relying on inspecting today's output (no baseline records currently appear) as proof of conformance, in place of verifying the path's own definition or its inherited eligibility rule
Conflating editorial freshness with discovery-novelty where a Clank has built editorial freshness as a concept at all
acceptance: Every default query, view, or API path whose semantics assert novelty — including secondary or derived such paths — excludes baseline/continuity-tagged records by including, or explicitly inheriting, a baseline-exclusion predicate (or an equivalent eligibility rule) as part of that path's own definition. The exclusion MUST be verifiable by inspecting the path's definition or its explicitly-inherited eligibility rule; relying on callers to filter, on filtering performed after the path's results are produced by logic external to the path, or on assumptions about what got written, does not conform.
A baseline-era record does not appear in a default novelty view even if it is the most recently observed row in the underlying table
An explicit override or review workflow (e.g. an operator deliberately inspecting baseline-era records) MAY surface them, provided doing so does not relabel them as novel in the process
Where editorial freshness is modeled, it is computed and stored/exposed separately from both discovery time and novelty status

evidence.summary: 'A reference that is merely absent from this database until today is not, by itself, evidence the manufacturer launched it today.' Alerts visibly mark such events 'novelty UNCONFIRMED'.

Two independent, dated, identically-shaped incidents: a correctly-written baseline flag was never consulted by the aggregation/display query, putting baseline-era records in front of genuine novelty (1,875 records at oem-radar; a comparable burst at watch-clank).
Baseline-gates-every-event-type design explicitly inherited from a named cross-Clank incident (smartphone-clank's 73-device contamination).
chinese-tech-wire architecturally separates editorial-freshness reporting from novelty scoring; korean-tech-wire explicitly names the same separation as necessary future work it hasn't built yet.

notes: Pass 1 draft (docs/data-ontology/pass1/dossier-c2-novelty-read-side-exclusion.md), from Pass 0B adjudication candidate C2 (docs/data-ontology/pass0/candidates/c2-novelty-read-side-exclusion.md), from Pass 0A clusters novelty-vs-discovery-time and editorial-freshness-vs-novelty (docs/data-ontology/pass0/clusters/). Deliberately mirrors STD-UI-COM-003's read-side-exclusion shape at the data layer rather than the UI layer — this standard governs the query/logic contract; STD-UI-COM-003 governs what the operator sees (COMPLEMENTARY, not duplicative, per Pass 2 review). Version 2 (Pass 2.5, docs/data-ontology/pass2/review.md's STD-DATA-COM-002 section): REVISE verdict applied exactly — acceptance criterion 1 strengthened to bind every default novelty-asserting path, including secondary/derived ones, requiring the exclusion be included or explicitly inherited as part of the path's own definition; two forbidden entries added (post-hoc filtering external to the path; relying on output inspection alone as proof of conformance). No other clause changed.
